title: The City Offer, With a Parent Who Is Getting Older
situation: You receive a strong job offer in another city. It would increase your income and responsibility, but one of your parents is getting older and currently lives close enough that you can help when needed. Nobody is asking you to stay, but you know distance will change what “being available” means.
intro: Every option costs something real. Choose the compromise you are most willing to live with — there is no correct answer.

options.title: Take the offer
options.description: Higher pay, bigger role, less presence.

options.title: Stay and renegotiate
costs: You may wonder what you missed

resultExample:
You chose presence over pace.
You prioritised:
 Being reachable when your family needs you.
You accepted:
 A slower professional climb, at least for now.
Values behind the choice:
 Presence — High
 Security — Medium–High
 Ambition — Medium
Another way to read it:
 Staying can be an act of care, but it can also be the option that asks the fewest uncomfortable questions. Leaving would not necessarily mean choosing career over family; it could also mean trusting that closeness is not measured only in kilometres.

title: The Promotion That Takes Your Evenings
situation: You are offered a promotion you have worked toward for years. The salary and title are better, but everyone in the role regularly works late and stays available on weekends.

options.title: Decline and stay where you are
Accept only with conditions
options.description: Negotiate the role before taking it.
gains: Tests how flexible the company really is

resultExample:
You chose growth with conditions.
You prioritised:
 Progress without giving unlimited access to your time.
You accepted:
 The possibility that the company may value availability more than your preferred boundary.
Another way to read it:
 Negotiating is not automatically the “balanced” choice. Sometimes it creates the comforting belief that you can have both options without fully accepting the culture of the role you are entering.

title: Lending Money to a Friend Who Has Struggled Before
situation: A close friend asks for a meaningful loan. They genuinely need help, but they have borrowed before and repayment has rarely happened on time.

options.title: Lend the full amount
gains: You act on your desire to help

options.title: Give a smaller amount as a gift
options.description: Help without creating debt between you.

options.title: Say no to money, help another way
options.description: Protect the friendship from a financial arrangement.

resultExample:
You chose support without debt.
You prioritised:
 Helping while keeping the friendship outside a lender–borrower dynamic.
You accepted:
 That your version of help may not be the version your friend wanted.
Another way to read it:
 A smaller gift can look like the safest compromise, but it can also postpone the harder question: whether repeated rescue is helping the person or simply making the pattern easier to continue.

title: Staying With a Partner Who Wants a Different Future
situation: Your relationship is good now, but you disagree about a major future decision. Neither of you expects to change your mind soon.

options.title: Stay and hope the future becomes clearer
End the relationship now
options.description: Protect long-term compatibility at an immediate emotional cost.
gains: Freedom to pursue the future you want
costs: Lose a relationship that currently works

options.title: Set a date to revisit the issue
options.description: Stay, but stop treating the question as indefinite.
gains: Time without pretending the conflict is solved

resultExample:
You chose the present, with a deadline.
You prioritised:
 Giving the relationship a real chance without treating uncertainty as permanent.
You accepted:
 That more time may make an eventual separation harder.
Another way to read it:
 A deadline can create clarity, but it can also become a sophisticated form of delay if neither person is using the time to learn anything new.

title: The House You Love but Should Barely Afford
situation: You find a home that fits almost everything you want. You can technically afford it, but the monthly cost would significantly reduce your savings and flexibility.

options.title: Take the home
costs: Less money for travel and hobbies

options.title: Choose a cheaper place
costs: You may keep comparing it to the first option

resultExample:
You chose flexibility over the perfect address.
You prioritised:
 Keeping room in your budget for the rest of your life.
You accepted:
 Living somewhere that may feel less exciting every day.
Another way to read it:
 Financial caution protects freedom, but excessive caution can turn money into something you preserve rather than something that supports the life you actually want.

title: Helping Family When You Are Already Exhausted
situation: A family member needs regular help for the next few months. You can provide it, but your own schedule is already full and you have started feeling exhausted.

options.title: Take on the responsibility
gains: You know the situation is handled
costs: Less time for your own responsibilities

options.title: Help less than requested
costs: Someone else must cover the gap

resultExample:
You chose to help without becoming the whole solution.
You prioritised:
 Being useful without making your availability unlimited.
You accepted:
 That another person may still believe you could have done more.
Another way to read it:
 A boundary can protect your energy, but “protecting capacity” can also become an easy phrase for avoiding difficult family responsibility. The important question is not whether you could do more, but whether doing more is sustainable and fairly shared.

title: The Friend Group That No Longer Feels Like Yours
situation: You have known the same group for years, but lately you often leave gatherings feeling disconnected. Nobody has done anything particularly wrong.

options.title: Keep showing up
costs: Time spent in connections that feel weaker

options.title: Gradually step back
options.description: Keep the relationships, change their place in your life.

options.title: Tell them how you feel
options.description: Create a chance for the friendships to change.
costs: Others may not feel the same
Could make the distance more visible

resultExample:
You chose change without a dramatic ending.
You prioritised:
 Making space for relationships that fit who you are now.
You accepted:
 That some old connections may weaken without anyone being at fault.
Another way to read it:
 Growing apart can be natural, but quietly stepping back also means deciding for everyone without giving the friendship a chance to adapt.

title: Telling the Truth When Silence Would Be Easier
situation: A friend asks for your honest opinion about a major decision they are excited about. You see serious problems they seem to be overlooking.

options.title: Tell them exactly what you think
Ask questions instead of giving a verdict
options.description: Help them examine the decision themselves.

options.title: Support them and stay quiet
options.description: Protect the relationship, keep your doubts private.
costs: They lose information you could have offered

resultExample:
You chose questions over a verdict.
You prioritised:
 Helping your friend think without taking the decision away from them.
You accepted:
 That subtlety may not communicate how serious your concern actually is.
Another way to read it:
 Questions can be respectful, but they can also become a way to avoid the discomfort of saying plainly what you believe.

title: Leaving a Good Job for Work That Matters More
situation: Your current job pays well and is comfortable. Another role would pay less but gives you work you find far more meaningful.

options.title: Stay temporarily with an exit plan

resultExample:
You chose preparation before purpose.
You prioritised:
 Making the transition without turning meaningful work into financial panic.
You accepted:
 Spending more time in a job you already know does not fit.
Another way to read it:
 Preparation can make a change safer. It can also become endlessly extendable. A plan without a date may simply be staying with better vocabulary.

title: Moving in Together Before You Feel Fully Ready
situation: Your partner wants to move in together. The relationship is strong, but you value having your own space and are not completely ready to give it up.

options.title: Move in now
options.description: Deepen the relationship, lose some independence.

options.title: Try a temporary arrangement
options.description: Test daily life without making it permanent.

resultExample:
You chose evidence before permanence.
You prioritised:
 Learning what everyday life together actually feels like.
You accepted:
 That a trial may feel less romantic and more deliberate than your partner hoped.
Another way to read it:
 Testing compatibility can be sensible, but not every part of a relationship can be made risk-free before commitment. At some point, choosing someone means accepting information you cannot have in advance.
